books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

stimulus.text:
This daguerreotype portrait of Frederick Douglass, made by Samuel J. Miller in 1847–1852, shows Douglass from the chest up, dressed as a respectable gentleman in a dark coat, white shirt, and bow tie, staring straight at the viewer with a stern expression.

"You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man." — Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845, on his fight with the overseer Edward Covey in August 1833.
stimulus.source_note: Portrait viewed before writing: Samuel J. Miller, daguerreotype of Frederick Douglass, 1847-1852, Art Institute of Chicago. Quotation verbatim from Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Miller daguerreotype of Douglass, 1847-1852, public domain
stem: The portrait and the Covey passage together best show Douglass’s strategy of

options.text: proving Black manhood both by living it and by showing it
asking white abolitionists to describe slavery for him in print
options.misconception: Douglass told his own story in his own words and image.

options.text: keeping his past as an enslaved man a secret
options.misconception: The Narrative told his past openly; the portrait advertised the man.

options.text: urging enslaved people to wait patiently for gradual emancipation
options.misconception: Douglass resisted Covey and demanded freedom; he did not counsel waiting.

rationales.A: The fight proves his manhood in life, and the portrait shows it to the public. Douglass lived the proof, then displayed it.
rationales.B: Douglass did not ask others to speak for him. He wrote the Narrative and sat for the portrait himself.
rationales.C: Nothing is secret. The Narrative tells his enslavement openly, and the portrait puts his face before the public.
rationales.D: Douglass did not counsel waiting. He fought Covey, escaped in 1838, and demanded freedom now.
rationales.general:
1. Take the passage. Douglass proves his manhood by fighting Covey and refusing to be broken.
2. Take the portrait. Douglass shows that manhood to the public, dressed as a gentleman and staring straight out.
3. Name the strategy. Live the proof, then show it.
Background: Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 and published the Narrative in 1845.
Remember: a life and a portrait can make the same argument in two forms.
